topic: sub:11|Formulas and equations|Medication dosages: Fried's, Young's and Clark's formulas

parts.latex:
A formula for the dosage in mL ($D$) of medicine required for a child aged between 1 and 12 years compared to an adult's dosage ($A$) is:

$$D=\dfrac{yA}{y+12}$$

where $y$ is the age of the child (years).

A 6-year-old child is to take 5 mL of a prescribed medicine three times per day.

What is the equivalent daily adult dosage of this medicine?

solutions.latex:
The daily child dosage is $D = 5\times 3 = 15$ mL.

Substitute $D=15$ and $y=6$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} 15 &= \dfrac{6A}{6+12} \\ 15\times 18 &= 6A \\ A &= \dfrac{270}{6} \\ &= 45 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the equivalent daily adult dosage is } 45 \text{ mL}$$

parts.latex:
A parent used Young's formula to calculate the required medication dosage for their child.

Young's formula is

$$\text{Dosage} = \dfrac{\text{Age of child (years)} \times \text{Adult dose}}{\text{Age of child (years)} + 12}.$$

They found that the child's dosage was one third of the adult dose.

How old is the child?

solutions.latex:
Let $a$ be the child's age in years and $d$ the adult dose. Young's formula gives the child's dose as one third of the adult dose:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}d &= \dfrac{ad}{a + 12} \\ \dfrac{a}{a + 12} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ 3a &= a + 12 \\ 2a &= 12 \\ a &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the child is 6 years old}$$
criteria: Creates a correct equation with the child's age as the only variable, or equivalent merit

6617.stem:
A formula for the dosage in mL ($D$) of medicine required for a child aged between 1 and 12 years ($y$) compared to an adult's dosage ($A$) is:

$$D=\dfrac{yA}{y+12}$$

parts.latex: Change the subject of this formula to $A$.

A 6-year-old child is to take 5 mL of a prescribed medicine three times per day.

What is the equivalent daily adult dosage for this medicine?

solutions.latex:
Make $A$ the subject of the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} D &= \dfrac{yA}{y+12} \\ D(y+12) &= yA \\ Dy+12D &= yA \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{Dy+12D}{y}$$
criteria: Multiplies both sides by $y+12$, or equivalent merit

6709.stem:
Young's rule is used to calculate the required dosage of medicine for children aged 1 to 12 years.

$$D = \dfrac{yA}{y + 12}$$

Where:

$D$ = Child dosage in milligrams

$y$ = Age of child in years

$A$ = Adult dosage in milligrams

parts.latex: What is the required dose for an 18-month-old child, if the adult dose is 72 mg?
The recommended dose for a 3-year-old child is 5 mg. What is the adult dosage using Young's rule?

solutions.latex:
The age is $18$ months $= 1.5$ years, so $y = 1.5$ and $A = 72$.
$$\begin{aligned} D &= \dfrac{yA}{y+12} \\ &= \dfrac{1.5 \times 72}{1.5 + 12} \\ &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the dose is } 8 \text{ mg}$$
criteria: Uses the formula with one error in substitution, or equivalent merit
